Inside an ONNX model

Source: vignettes/articles/onnx.Rmd
onnx.Rmd

An ONNX model file is one Protocol Buffers message, a ModelProto: the network’s graph, its operators and every trained weight. PyTorch, TensorFlow and scikit-learn all export to it, and runtimes from phones to browsers load it. Because it is plain protobuf, zuproto can read one without any machine-learning library. This article opens a small handwritten-digit classifier and looks at its layers and weights.

The output below comes from a run on 27 October 2026. The code is not run when the site is built.

library(zuproto)

The schema

The schema is onnx.proto, from the onnx repository. protoc, the protobuf compiler, turns it into a descriptor set, which is what zuproto reads. zuproto itself does not need protoc: on macOS, brew install protobuf; on Debian and Ubuntu, apt install protobuf-compiler.

dir <- tempfile("onnx-")
dir.create(dir)
proto <- file.path(dir, "onnx.proto")
desc <- file.path(dir, "onnx.binpb")

download.file(
  "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/onnx/onnx/v1.23.2/onnx/onnx.proto",
  proto,
  quiet = TRUE
)
system2("protoc", c(
  paste0("--proto_path=", dir),
  paste0("--descriptor_set_out=", desc),
  proto
))
pool <- proto_pool(desc)

The model

The model is MNIST from the ONNX Model Zoo: a small convolutional network that reads a 28 by 28 grey image of a digit. The file is 26 kB.

model <- file.path(dir, "mnist-12.onnx")
download.file(
  paste0(
    "https://media.githubusercontent.com/media/onnx/models/",
    "c5cae0f1942c8d7727372c7b1f6b485aa39e4421/",
    "validated/vision/classification/mnist/model/mnist-12.onnx"
  ),
  model,
  mode = "wb",
  quiet = TRUE
)
m <- proto_decode(model, "onnx.ModelProto", pool, defaults = FALSE)

defaults = FALSE leaves out the fields the file does not set, which keeps the result small. Everything except the graph is metadata: who wrote the file, and which version of the ONNX operator set it uses.

str(m[names(m) != "graph"])
#> List of 6
#>  $ ir_version      : num 7
#>  $ opset_import    :List of 1
#>   ..$ :List of 2
#>   .. ..$ domain : chr ""
#>   .. ..$ version: num 12
#>  $ producer_name   : chr "CNTK"
#>  $ producer_version: chr "2.5.1"
#>  $ domain          : chr "ai.cntk"
#>  $ model_version   : num 1

The graph as a table

The graph is a list of nodes. Each node applies one operator to named inputs and writes named outputs, and the names wire the nodes together. A data frame with one row per node reads like the network’s layer list.

g <- m$graph
nodes <- data.frame(
  name = vapply(g$node, \(n) n$name, ""),
  op = vapply(g$node, \(n) n$op_type, ""),
  inputs = vapply(g$node, \(n) paste(n$input, collapse = ", "), ""),
  output = vapply(g$node, \(n) paste(n$output, collapse = ", "), "")
)
nodes[, c("name", "op", "inputs")]
#>                 name      op
#> 1      Convolution28    Conv
#> 2             Plus30     Add
#> 3             ReLU32    Relu
#> 4          Pooling66 MaxPool
#> 5     Convolution110    Conv
#> 6            Plus112     Add
#> 7            ReLU114    Relu
#> 8         Pooling160 MaxPool
#> 9  Times212_reshape0 Reshape
#> 10 Times212_reshape1 Reshape
#> 11          Times212  MatMul
#> 12           Plus214     Add
#>                                                     inputs
#> 1                                       Input3, Parameter5
#> 2                       Convolution28_Output_0, Parameter6
#> 3                                          Plus30_Output_0
#> 4                                          ReLU32_Output_0
#> 5                          Pooling66_Output_0, Parameter87
#> 6                     Convolution110_Output_0, Parameter88
#> 7                                         Plus112_Output_0
#> 8                                         ReLU114_Output_0
#> 9  Pooling160_Output_0, Pooling160_Output_0_reshape0_shape
#> 10               Parameter193, Parameter193_reshape1_shape
#> 11     Pooling160_Output_0_reshape0, Parameter193_reshape1
#> 12                         Times212_Output_0, Parameter194

Operator settings are attributes. A string attribute is bytes in the schema, so it decodes to a raw vector.

conv <- g$node[[1]]
vapply(conv$attribute, \(a) a$name, "")
#> [1] "kernel_shape" "strides"      "auto_pad"     "group"        "dilations"
rawToChar(conv$attribute[[3]]$s)
#> [1] "SAME_UPPER"

Inputs and outputs

A tensor’s element type is an int32 in the schema, holding a number from the TensorProto.DataType enum. proto_enums() turns the number into its name.

dtypes <- proto_enums(pool, "onnx.TensorProto.DataType")
head(dtypes)
#>        name number
#> 1 UNDEFINED      0
#> 2     FLOAT      1
#> 3     UINT8      2
#> 4      INT8      3
#> 5    UINT16      4
#> 6     INT16      5

describe <- function(v) {
  t <- v$type$tensor_type
  data.frame(
    name = v$name,
    type = dtypes$name[match(t$elem_type, dtypes$number)],
    shape = paste(vapply(t$shape$dim, \(d) d$dim_value, 0), collapse = " x ")
  )
}
do.call(rbind, lapply(c(g$input, g$output), describe))
#>               name  type           shape
#> 1           Input3 FLOAT 1 x 1 x 28 x 28
#> 2 Plus214_Output_0 FLOAT          1 x 10

The input is one image of one channel, 28 by 28 pixels; the output is ten scores, one per digit.

The weights

The trained weights are the graph’s initializers, tensors stored in the file. ONNX keeps the numbers in a typed field (float_data, int64_data) or as packed little-endian bytes (raw_data); this file uses the typed fields. A small helper turns either into an R array.

tensor_array <- function(t) {
  values <- if (length(t$raw_data) > 0) {
    readBin(t$raw_data, "double", n = prod(t$dims), size = 4, endian = "little")
  } else if (length(t$float_data) > 0) {
    t$float_data
  } else {
    t$int64_data
  }
  # ONNX stores tensors row-major, R arrays are column-major.
  if (length(t$dims) > 1) {
    aperm(array(values, rev(t$dims)))
  } else {
    values
  }
}

weights <- lapply(g$initializer, tensor_array)
names(weights) <- vapply(g$initializer, \(t) t$name, "")
shape <- \(w) paste(if (is.null(dim(w))) length(w) else dim(w), collapse = " x ")
vapply(weights, shape, "")
#>                       Parameter193                        Parameter87 
#>                  "16 x 4 x 4 x 10"                   "16 x 8 x 5 x 5" 
#>                         Parameter5                         Parameter6 
#>                    "8 x 1 x 5 x 5"                        "8 x 1 x 1" 
#>                        Parameter88 Pooling160_Output_0_reshape0_shape 
#>                       "16 x 1 x 1"                                "2" 
#>        Parameter193_reshape1_shape                       Parameter194 
#>                                "2"                           "1 x 10"
sum(lengths(weights))
#> [1] 5998

The network has under six thousand weights. The first convolution has eight filters of 5 by 5 pixels; drawn as images, they are the patterns the network looks for in a digit.

filters <- weights[["Parameter5"]] # 8 x 1 x 5 x 5
op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 8), mar = c(0.2, 0.2, 0.2, 0.2))
for (k in 1:8) {
  w <- filters[k, 1, , ]
  image(t(w[5:1, ]), col = gray.colors(32), axes = FALSE, asp = 1)
}

plot of chunk filters 

par(op)

Writing a model back

proto_encode() is the inverse of proto_decode(). Here the model gains a description and a metadata entry, and is written to a new file. ONNX’s own checker accepts the file, and onnxruntime gives the same scores for it as for the original.

m$doc_string <- "MNIST digit classifier, annotated in R"
m$metadata_props <- list(list(key = "source", value = "ONNX Model Zoo"))
out <- file.path(dir, "mnist-annotated.onnx")
writeBin(proto_encode(m, "onnx.ModelProto", pool), out)

again <- proto_decode(out, "onnx.ModelProto", pool, defaults = FALSE)
again$doc_string
#> [1] "MNIST digit classifier, annotated in R"
identical(again$graph, m$graph)
#> [1] TRUE
